question.text: On a highway of five or more lanes with a shared center turn lane, who must stop for a school bus?

answer.text: On a highway of five or more lanes with a shared center turn lane, vehicles in the lanes behind a stopped school bus must stop fully, while opposite-direction traffic is not legally required to.

teaching.text: On five-plus lanes with a center turn lane, only lanes behind the school bus must stop. Remember: lanes behind the bus stop.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: On a highway of five or more lanes with a shared center turn lane, vehicles in the lanes behind a stopped school bus must stop fully, while opposite-direction traffic is not legally required to.

question.text: What follows from breaking school bus traffic laws?

answer.text: Breaking school bus traffic laws carries serious legal consequences.

teaching.text: School bus law violations carry serious legal consequences. Remember: bus laws carry weight.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Breaking school bus traffic laws carries serious legal consequences.

question.text: When can a train reach a crossing, and what should you obey?

answer.text: A train can reach a crossing at any hour, so approach with caution and obey every warning device, light, gate and sign.

teaching.text: Trains can come at any hour, so obey every crossing device. Remember: trains any hour.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A train can reach a crossing at any hour, so approach with caution and obey every warning device, light, gate and sign.

question.text: Why does a train look slower than it is, and how far does a freight train need to stop?

answer.text: A train's large size makes it look slower than it really is, and an average freight train at fifty-five miles per hour needs about one mile to stop.

teaching.text: Trains look slower than they are, and a freight train at fifty-five needs about a mile to stop. Remember: trains deceive and need a mile.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A train's large size makes it look slower than it really is, and an average freight train at fifty-five miles per hour needs about one mile to stop.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: trains deceive and need a mile

question.text: Why must you judge a train's speed and distance carefully?

answer.text: A train looks slower than it is, and a freight train at fifty-five miles per hour needs about a mile to stop, so judge its speed and distance carefully.

teaching.text: Judge a train's speed and distance carefully, because size fools the eye. Remember: slow-looking, far to stop.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A train looks slower than it is, and a freight train at fifty-five miles per hour needs about a mile to stop, so judge its speed and distance carefully.

question.text: What should you do at a crossing without flashing lights or gates?

answer.text: At a crossing without flashing lights or gates, stop beforehand if needed to check for trains.

teaching.text: With no lights or gates, stop if needed to check for trains. Remember: stop and check if needed.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: At a crossing without flashing lights or gates, stop beforehand if needed to check for trains.

question.text: When may you enter a railroad crossing?

answer.text: It is illegal and very dangerous to stop on the tracks; enter a crossing only once you know the rails are clear and your car fits fully past them, and with several tracks watch for a second train.

teaching.text: Never stop on the tracks; cross only when your whole car fits past them. Remember: never stop on tracks.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: It is illegal and very dangerous to stop on the tracks; enter a crossing only once you know the rails are clear and your car fits fully past them, and with several tracks watch for a second train.

question.text: What does the round advance warning sign tell you?

answer.text: The round advance warning sign, the only round traffic sign, tells you a railroad crossing is ahead early enough for you to stop if needed.

teaching.text: The round advance sign warns of a crossing in time to stop. Remember: round sign, crossing ahead.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The round advance warning sign, the only round traffic sign, tells you a railroad crossing is ahead early enough for you to stop if needed.

question.text: Where do you wait for a passing train, and why that distance?

answer.text: Railroad pavement markings show an R X R and a stop line; wait behind the line for a passing train, or at least ten feet from the tracks if no line shows, because trains overhang the rails by three feet.

teaching.text: Wait behind the stop line, because trains overhang the rails by three feet. Remember: wait behind the line.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Railroad pavement markings show an R X R and a stop line; wait behind the line for a passing train, or at least ten feet from the tracks if no line shows, because trains overhang the rails by three feet.

question.text: With no stop line painted, how far from the rails should you stay?

answer.text: With no stop line painted, keep at least ten feet from the rails, because a train overhangs the tracks by three feet.

teaching.text: With no stop line, stay at least ten feet from the rails. Remember: ten feet back.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: With no stop line painted, keep at least ten feet from the rails, because a train overhangs the tracks by three feet.

question.text: What warns you at a crossing in a designated quiet zone?

answer.text: In a designated quiet zone a No Train Horn sign hangs below the advance warning sign, horns do not sound, and the flashing lights and gates are your warning.

teaching.text: In quiet zones, horns are silent, so lights and gates are your warning. Remember: no horn, watch lights.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: In a designated quiet zone a No Train Horn sign hangs below the advance warning sign, horns do not sound, and the flashing lights and gates are your warning.

question.text: How do you treat a railroad crossbuck?

answer.text: Treat a crossbuck like a yield sign; a sign beneath it gives the number of tracks when there is more than one, and the crossbuck is normally a caution sign that becomes regulatory when a train approaches.

teaching.text: A crossbuck works like a yield sign and becomes regulatory when a train approaches. Remember: crossbuck means yield.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Treat a crossbuck like a yield sign; a sign beneath it gives the number of tracks when there is more than one, and the crossbuck is normally a caution sign that becomes regulatory when a train approaches.

question.text: Which vehicles must stop at most railroad crossings?

answer.text: Commercial buses and hazardous-materials trucks must stop at most crossings, so be ready to stop when following one.

teaching.text: Be ready to stop behind commercial buses and hazmat trucks at crossings. Remember: buses and hazmat stop.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Commercial buses and hazardous-materials trucks must stop at most crossings, so be ready to stop when following one.

question.text: What must you do when crossing lights flash?

answer.text: Always stop when crossing lights flash and do not cross until they stop flashing.

teaching.text: Stop for flashing crossing lights and wait until they stop. Remember: flashing lights, always stop.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Always stop when crossing lights flash and do not cross until they stop flashing.

question.text: What does it mean when crossing gates are down?

answer.text: Where gates are used with flashing lights, the road is closed while the gates are down; wait until the gates rise and the lights stop flashing.

teaching.text: Lowered gates close the road until they rise and the lights stop. Remember: gates down, road closed.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Where gates are used with flashing lights, the road is closed while the gates are down; wait until the gates rise and the lights stop flashing.

question.text: How does a crossbuck differ from flashing lights and lowered gates?

answer.text: A crossbuck is a yield-type sign that becomes regulatory as a train approaches, while flashing lights and lowered gates always mean stop.

teaching.text: Crossbucks mean yield; flashing lights and gates always mean stop. Remember: yield sign versus stop.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A crossbuck is a yield-type sign that becomes regulatory as a train approaches, while flashing lights and lowered gates always mean stop.

question.text: How does the round advance warning sign differ from a crossbuck?

answer.text: The round advance warning sign only tells you a crossing is ahead in time to stop, while the crossbuck carries a yield duty.

teaching.text: The round sign warns ahead; the crossbuck carries the yield duty. Remember: warning first, yield at crossbuck.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The round advance warning sign only tells you a crossing is ahead in time to stop, while the crossbuck carries a yield duty.

question.text: What should you do if your car stalls on the tracks?

answer.text: If your car stalls on the rails, have all occupants leave and move well away right away, train or no train in view, then phone the number on the blue Emergency Notification sign or local law enforcement.

teaching.text: Stalled on the tracks? Get everyone out and away, then call. Remember: get out, then call.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If your car stalls on the rails, have all occupants leave and move well away right away, train or no train in view, then phone the number on the blue Emergency Notification sign or local law enforcement.

question.text: Where is the blue Emergency Notification System sign, and what does it list?

answer.text: Every public highway-rail grade crossing has a blue Emergency Notification System sign, usually on the post below the crossbuck, with a phone number answered at all hours.

teaching.text: Every public crossing has a blue ENS sign with a number answered at all hours. Remember: blue sign, number always answered.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Every public highway-rail grade crossing has a blue Emergency Notification System sign, usually on the post below the crossbuck, with a phone number answered at all hours.

question.text: What is the ENS number for, and why give the crossing number?

answer.text: The ENS number is for emergencies that would require stopping a train, and giving the DOT crossing number on the sign lets the dispatcher pinpoint the crossing and warn trains.

teaching.text: Give the DOT crossing number so the dispatcher can warn trains. Remember: crossing number pinpoints you.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The ENS number is for emergencies that would require stopping a train, and giving the DOT crossing number on the sign lets the dispatcher pinpoint the crossing and warn trains.

question.text: In what order do you act if your car stalls on the tracks?

answer.text: A stalled car on the tracks calls for getting everyone out and away first and phoning the ENS number or police second.

teaching.text: People out and away first, phone call second. Remember: people out first.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A stalled car on the tracks calls for getting everyone out and away first and phoning the ENS number or police second.

question.text: How does RTD light rail run on streets?

answer.text: RTD runs light rail vehicles in the Denver metro area, sometimes in the same direction as traffic and sometimes against it, and on streets they obey all signals and signs with the same rights and duties as other motorists.

teaching.text: RTD light rail runs with or against traffic and obeys signals like other motorists. Remember: light rail obeys signals.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: RTD runs light rail vehicles in the Denver metro area, sometimes in the same direction as traffic and sometimes against it, and on streets they obey all signals and signs with the same rights and duties as other motorists.

question.text: Why should you never turn in front of a light rail car?

answer.text: A light rail car can weigh up to forty tons and cannot stop quickly, so never turn in front of one or across its tracks without checking every direction.

teaching.text: Light rail can weigh up to forty tons and cannot stop quickly, so never turn in front of it. Remember: forty tons, slow to stop.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A light rail car can weigh up to forty tons and cannot stop quickly, so never turn in front of one or across its tracks without checking every direction.

question.text: What should you watch for around stopped light rail vehicles?

answer.text: Watch for riders getting on and off a stopped light rail vehicle, and stay alert because buildings and plants can hide light rail vehicles.

teaching.text: Watch for riders, and remember buildings and plants can hide trains. Remember: riders and hidden trains.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Watch for riders getting on and off a stopped light rail vehicle, and stay alert because buildings and plants can hide light rail vehicles.

question.text: What do light rail crossing lights, warning lights and gates mean?

answer.text: Light rail crossings may use regular traffic lights, warning lights or gates with arms, and all of them mean stop and do not cross the tracks.

teaching.text: Every light rail crossing device means stop and do not cross. Remember: all mean stop.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Light rail crossings may use regular traffic lights, warning lights or gates with arms, and all of them mean stop and do not cross the tracks.

question.text: Why should you never drive around light rail gates?

answer.text: Never drive around light rail gates, even right after a train passes, because another may be coming from the other direction.

teaching.text: Never drive around light rail gates, even right after a train. Remember: another train may come.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Never drive around light rail gates, even right after a train passes, because another may be coming from the other direction.

question.text: How should you treat light rail overhead wires?

answer.text: Light rail overhead wires sit at a standard eighteen feet, six inches above the track center, so know your vehicle height, assume any hanging wire is live and never touch it or anything touching it.

teaching.text: Know your vehicle height, and treat every hanging wire as live. Remember: every wire is live.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Light rail overhead wires sit at a standard eighteen feet, six inches above the track center, so know your vehicle height, assume any hanging wire is live and never touch it or anything touching it.

question.text: How do you report a hanging wire or faulty light rail device?

answer.text: Report a hanging overhead wire or faulty light rail safety device by calling nine one one or RTD.

teaching.text: Report hanging wires or faulty devices to nine-one-one or RTD. Remember: call nine-one-one or RTD.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Report a hanging overhead wire or faulty light rail safety device by calling nine one one or RTD.

question.text: How are bicycles treated on the roadway?

answer.text: Bicycles are vehicles on the roadway, and their riders generally follow the same rules of the road with many of the same rights and duties as motorists.

teaching.text: Bicycles are vehicles whose riders follow the rules of the road. Remember: bikes follow the rules.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Bicycles are vehicles on the roadway, and their riders generally follow the same rules of the road with many of the same rights and duties as motorists.

question.text: How can local ordinances treat bicyclists differently?

answer.text: Some local ordinances treat bicyclists differently, for example letting them ride on sidewalks and in crosswalks with pedestrian rights and duties.

teaching.text: Local ordinances may let riders use sidewalks and crosswalks as pedestrians. Remember: local rules may differ.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Some local ordinances treat bicyclists differently, for example letting them ride on sidewalks and in crosswalks with pedestrian rights and duties.

question.text: Is there one statewide rule for riding bicycles on sidewalks?

answer.text: Whether bicyclists may ride on sidewalks depends on local ordinance, not one statewide rule.

teaching.text: Sidewalk riding depends on local ordinance. Remember: sidewalk rules are local.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Whether bicyclists may ride on sidewalks depends on local ordinance, not one statewide rule.

question.text: Why should you actively look for bicyclists?

answer.text: Bicyclists are smaller and more vulnerable than people in vehicles and vary in skill, and some are children, so look for them actively and use caution when approaching or passing.

teaching.text: Riders are vulnerable and vary in skill, so look for them actively. Remember: riders are vulnerable.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Bicyclists are smaller and more vulnerable than people in vehicles and vary in skill, and some are children, so look for them actively and use caution when approaching or passing.

question.text: Where should bicyclists ride, and when may they take the lane center?

answer.text: Bicyclists should ride as far right as they judge safe, but they may take the center of the lane for visibility, on narrow roads, or to avoid car door zones, broken glass or drainage grates.

teaching.text: Riders keep right when safe but may take the lane center for visibility or hazards. Remember: right, unless unsafe.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Bicyclists should ride as far right as they judge safe, but they may take the center of the lane for visibility, on narrow roads, or to avoid car door zones, broken glass or drainage grates.

question.text: When may bicyclists ride side by side?

answer.text: Bicyclists may ride side by side when they are not blocking normal, reasonable traffic flow, which can make them more visible and quicker to pass.

teaching.text: Riders may go side by side when they do not block normal traffic. Remember: side by side if not blocking.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Bicyclists may ride side by side when they are not blocking normal, reasonable traffic flow, which can make them more visible and quicker to pass.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: side by side if not blocking

question.text: Can a bicyclist riding mid-lane or side by side be within the law?

answer.text: A bicyclist in the center of the lane or riding side by side may be within the law, for visibility or hazard avoidance, as long as normal traffic is not impeded.

teaching.text: A mid-lane or side-by-side rider may be riding within the law. Remember: mid-lane can be legal.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A bicyclist in the center of the lane or riding side by side may be within the law, for visibility or hazard avoidance, as long as normal traffic is not impeded.

question.text: How much room must you give a bicyclist when passing, even in a bike lane?

answer.text: When passing a bicyclist, even one in a bike lane, give at least three feet from the outermost part of your vehicle or attachments; if you cannot, slow down and stay behind until it is safe.

teaching.text: Give at least three feet from your outermost part, or stay behind. Remember: three feet or wait.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When passing a bicyclist, even one in a bike lane, give at least three feet from the outermost part of your vehicle or attachments; if you cannot, slow down and stay behind until it is safe.

question.text: When may you cross a double yellow line to pass a bicyclist?

answer.text: Crossing a double yellow line with no oncoming traffic is legal when needed to give a bicyclist the three-foot passing gap.

teaching.text: Crossing a double yellow to give three feet is legal when nothing is oncoming. Remember: cross yellow for three feet.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Crossing a double yellow line with no oncoming traffic is legal when needed to give a bicyclist the three-foot passing gap.

question.text: What should you do if you cannot give a bicyclist three feet?

answer.text: The three-foot bicyclist gap allows briefly crossing a double yellow line when nothing is oncoming; if three feet is impossible, stay behind the rider.

teaching.text: If three feet is impossible, wait behind the rider. Remember: stay behind the rider.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The three-foot bicyclist gap allows briefly crossing a double yellow line when nothing is oncoming; if three feet is impossible, stay behind the rider.

question.text: How should you treat bicyclists in intersections?

answer.text: Yield to bicyclists in intersections as you would to pedestrians and other vehicles.

teaching.text: Yield to bicyclists in intersections like anyone else. Remember: yield like to anyone.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Yield to bicyclists in intersections as you would to pedestrians and other vehicles.

question.text: Who has the right of way in a bike lane, and what may drivers not do there?

answer.text: Bicyclists have the right-of-way in a bike lane, the lane continues through intersections even without paint, and drivers may not stop, park or drive in a bike lane or path.

teaching.text: Bike lanes belong to bicyclists, even through intersections. Remember: bike lane belongs to bikes.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Bicyclists have the right-of-way in a bike lane, the lane continues through intersections even without paint, and drivers may not stop, park or drive in a bike lane or path.

question.text: How do you avoid the common left-turn crash with a cyclist?

answer.text: To avoid the common left-turn crash with an oncoming cyclist, look for riders on the shoulder, at the lane edge or behind other vehicles and judge their speed and distance before turning.

teaching.text: Look for riders on the shoulder and lane edge, and judge their speed before turning left. Remember: look for riders first.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: To avoid the common left-turn crash with an oncoming cyclist, look for riders on the shoulder, at the lane edge or behind other vehicles and judge their speed and distance before turning.

question.text: How do you avoid stop-sign and signal crashes with cyclists?

answer.text: To avoid stop-sign and signal crashes, stop first, then enter the intersection only after looking for and yielding to others.

teaching.text: Stop first, then look and yield before entering. Remember: stop, look, yield.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: To avoid stop-sign and signal crashes, stop first, then enter the intersection only after looking for and yielding to others.

question.text: What should you do before opening your car door into the road?

answer.text: Before opening a door into the roadway, check behind for passing riders or vehicles, and try opening it with the hand farther from the door.

teaching.text: Check behind before opening a door, and use your far hand. Remember: far hand opens door.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Before opening a door into the roadway, check behind for passing riders or vehicles, and try opening it with the hand farther from the door.

question.text: How should you turn right when a cyclist is going straight?

answer.text: When turning right, yield and let a cyclist going straight clear the intersection first, and turn from close to the curb so no rider can pass unsafely on your right.

teaching.text: Let a straight-going cyclist clear before your right turn, and turn close to the curb. Remember: let the rider clear.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When turning right, yield and let a cyclist going straight clear the intersection first, and turn from close to the curb so no rider can pass unsafely on your right.

question.text: What should you check when pulling out of a driveway?

answer.text: When pulling out of a driveway, check both directions and past the curb or driveway for riders on the road, sidewalk or bike path.

teaching.text: Check both ways and past the curb before leaving a driveway. Remember: check past the curb.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When pulling out of a driveway, check both directions and past the curb or driveway for riders on the road, sidewalk or bike path.
